summary: SOD modifies on-policy distillation for small models doing tool-integrated reasoning with a Python interpreter. It reweights the teacher's token-level signal per step by student-teacher divergence, so supervision is damped after an erroneous tool call has pushed the student off-distribution. Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B students distilled from a GRPO-tuned Qwen3-4B teacher beat SFT, GRPO, OPD and OPSD baselines on AIME 2024/2025, GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench.

claims.claim: Up to 20.86% improvement over the second-best baseline
claims.evidence: Table 1: 0.6B average 24.22 (SOD) vs 20.04 (OPD), a relative gain of 20.86%, i.e. about 4.2 absolute points. 1.7B: 42.98 vs 36.27 (18.50% relative). The abstract's 'improvement' is relative, not absolute.

claims.claim: 0.6B student reaches 26.13% on AIME 2025, 'first sub-billion model' at this level
claims.evidence: Table 1: 26.13 ± 1.07 (avg@32 over 5 runs). The 'first' claim is asserted without a survey or comparison.

claims.claim: Naive OPD fails under tool-induced state drift; step-wise reweighting fixes it
claims.evidence: Propositions 1-2 (§4.1); training dynamics in Fig. 4 (OPD 1.7B peaks then degrades); ablation of six variants (§5.3); 14B-teacher generalization (§5.4, Fig. 3).

patterns.note: Distillation-based post-training of small tool-using models, with seeds and ablations; limited to Python-interpreter TIR.
Makes small models more capable, which could feed a cheap tier in a cascade; routing itself is not studied.

methodology.sample: 4 benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench); 3k SFT + 30k RL training examples
methodology.baselines: Vanilla, SFT, GRPO, OPD, OPSD-gt, OPSD-hint under one shared config. At 0.6B, SFT and GRPO score below the untrained model (e.g. AIME24 7.71 → 5.67 / 4.06), which suggests the baselines were not tuned per method.
methodology.models: Qwen3 family only (0.6B/1.7B students; 4B and 14B teachers)
methodology.variance: avg@32 samples, 5 seeds, ± reported in Table 1
methodology.ablations: Six variants on step reweighting and objective (§5.3); teacher scale (§5.4)
methodology.contamination_controls: LiveCodeBench is contamination-aware; AIME 2024/2025 overlap with Qwen3 pretraining is not discussed

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/YoungZ365/SOD; HF collection youngzhong/sod

biases.detail: Python interpreter is the only tool; acknowledged that web/API agents may drift differently.
Shared hyperparameters 'to isolate the effect' leave SFT/GRPO below the vanilla model at 0.6B.
AIME results on Qwen3 are not checked for training-data overlap.

coi.affiliations: Zhejiang University, Tencent (Large Language Model Department), USTC, National University of Singapore; work done during a Tencent internship
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None of Tencent's; Qwen3 (Alibaba) open models used
coi.detail: Vendor-affiliated authors evaluating a training method on a competitor's open models; no product promotion.

verdict_reason: Sound ML evaluation with 5 seeds, variance, ablations, two teacher scales and released code. It is narrow (one model family, Python interpreter, math/science/competitive coding) and its baselines may be undertuned. Admitted only as background on agent-model training; it is very weakly relevant to harness design.
applicability: Little direct transfer. A Java backend team building a harness across mixed agent hosts will not distill its own sub-2B tool-using models, and the paper's tasks (AIME, GPQA, LiveCodeBench in Python) do not resemble multi-repo ingestion work or spec-driven development. The only takeaway is indirect: small models fail by cascading errors after a bad tool call. That argues for cheap, early verifier checks (compile or test after each tool action) if a small or cheap model tier is ever used.

conflicts_with.detail: That paper (per its abstract) finds the update direction on the small subset of tokens with large teacher-student disagreement is what makes OPD work. SOD instead attenuates distillation in high-divergence steps. The granularities differ (token vs step), but the two make opposing prescriptions about high-divergence regions.
